questions.q: Define atomic number (Z) and mass number (A) using the standard notation \(^{A}_{Z}\text{X}\). State the relationship between Z, A, and the number of neutrons (n).
questions.a: Atomic number (Z) = number of protons in the nucleus = number of electrons in a neutral atom. Mass number (A) = total number of nucleons = number of protons + number of neutrons. Relationship: A = Z + n, so n = A – Z. In notation \(^{A}_{Z}\text{X}\), A is the left superscript, Z is the left subscript. A wrong answer (e.g., swapping Z and A, or saying Z = neutrons) reveals the student confuses the two definitions or misremembers the notation layout — a critical error for writing nuclear symbols in board exams.

questions.q: A neutral atom has 17 protons and 18 neutrons. Write its complete symbol \(^{A}_{Z}\text{X}\) and name the element. Then write the symbol for the ion formed when this atom gains one electron.
questions.a: Protons = 17 → Z = 17 (chlorine, Cl). Neutrons = 18 → A = 17 + 18 = 35. Neutral atom: \(^{35}_{17}\text{Cl}\). After gaining one electron, it has 18 electrons and 17 protons → charge = –1. Ion symbol: \(^{35}_{17}\text{Cl}^-\). A wrong answer (e.g., writing \(^{17}_{35}\text{Cl}\) or \(^{35}_{17}\text{Cl}^+\)) reveals the student either reverses the superscript/subscript positions or misunderstands that gaining electrons creates a negative charge — both are common board-exam mistakes.

questions.q: Calculate the number of protons, neutrons, and electrons in \(^{80}_{35}\text{Br}^-\). Show all steps.
questions.a: Step 1: Identify Z = 35 (subscript) → protons = 35. Step 2: Identify A = 80 (superscript) → mass number = 80. Step 3: Neutrons = A – Z = 80 – 35 = 45. Step 4: Charge is –1 → electrons = protons + 1 = 35 + 1 = 36. Final answer: protons = 35, neutrons = 45, electrons = 36. A wrong answer (e.g., electrons = 35 or neutrons = 35) reveals the student either ignores the ion charge when counting electrons or confuses Z with neutron number — indicating they haven't internalised that Z always equals protons, never neutrons.

questions.q: Two species are given: \(^{14}_{6}\text{C}\) and \(^{14}_{7}\text{N}\). Are they isotopes, isobars, or neither? Justify your answer using the definitions of Z and A.
questions.a: They are isobars. \(^{14}_{6}\text{C}\) has Z = 6, A = 14. \(^{14}_{7}\text{N}\) has Z = 7, A = 14. Same mass number (A = 14) but different atomic numbers (Z = 6 vs 7) → isobars by definition. Isotopes would require same Z, different A. A wrong answer (e.g., calling them isotopes) reveals the student memorised "same mass number = isotopes" without understanding that isotopes share Z (same element) while isobars share A (different elements) — a conceptual confusion that undermines nuclear chemistry.

questions.q: A student writes the symbol for a magnesium ion with 12 protons, 12 neutrons, and 10 electrons as \(^{24}_{12}\text{Mg}^{2-}\). Evaluate this symbol and correct it if necessary.
questions.a: The symbol is incorrect. Protons = 12 → Z = 12 (Mg). Neutrons = 12 → A = 12 + 12 = 24. Electrons = 10, protons = 12 → net charge = +2 (cation), not –2. Correct symbol: \(^{24}_{12}\text{Mg}^{2+}\). The student's error shows they think "fewer electrons = negative charge" — a sign-reversal misconception. In board exams, such charge errors lose full marks even if A and Z are correct.

questions.q: Design a set of three nuclear symbols \(^{A}_{Z}\text{X}\) that represent: (i) an isotope of carbon-12, (ii) an isobar of carbon-12, and (iii) a different element with the same neutron number as carbon-12. Explain your reasoning for each.
questions.a: (i) Isotope of \(^{12}_{6}\text{C}\): same Z = 6, different A. Example: \(^{13}_{6}\text{C}\) (7 neutrons) or \(^{14}_{6}\text{C}\) (8 neutrons). (ii) Isobar of \(^{12}_{6}\text{C}\): same A = 12, different Z. Example: \(^{12}_{5}\text{B}\) or \(^{12}_{7}\text{N}\). (iii) Same neutron number as \(^{12}_{6}\text{C}\) (which has n = 12 – 6 = 6): choose any element with n = 6. Example: \(^{13}_{7}\text{N}\) (Z=7, n=6) or \(^{14}_{8}\text{O}\) (Z=8, n=6). A poor answer (e.g., giving \(^{12}_{6}\text{C}\) itself for (i) or confusing the categories) reveals the student cannot independently manipulate Z, A, and n — they only recognise definitions passively.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Atomic number (Z) is the number of protons in the nucleus of an atom, which uniquely ______ an element and equals the number of electrons in a neutral atom.

Fill in the blank: Next, hold up a sample of carbon (like graphite from a pencil) and explain that while all carbon atoms have 6 protons, some have 6 neutrons and others 7 or 8 — introducing mass number ______.
What is Atomic number (Z)? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Atomic number (Z) is the number of protons in the nucleus of an atom, which uniquely identifies an element and equals the number of electrons in a neutral atom.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Atomic number (Z)?
questions.a: They also assume atomic number equals neutron number for neutral atoms, or that the charge on an ion is determined by the neutron count.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Next, hold up a sample of carbon (like graphite from a pencil) and explain that while all carbon atoms have 6 protons, some have 6 neutrons and others 7 or 8 — ______ mass number variation.
